explanation: Fires most on the decimal point inside a decimal number (e.g. '23[[.]]3%', '12[[.]]9 inches', '9[[.]]3.0'), especially in statistics, measurements, percentages and version numbers. It also fires moderately on a mixed set of words that start a fixed technical phrase ('organic' in 'organic synthesis/solvent', 'central' nervous system, 'directional' selection, 'primary' DNA sequence, 'vehicle', 'I[-]65'). Ordinary prose tokens fire weakly or not at all.

Fires on a word-piece in the middle of a word that has been split into subword tokens, mostly pieces near 'ne', 'te' or 'ine' (calc[ine]urin, sensor[ine]ural, Ne-dlands, NE-VADA, [Te]er, [Pod]laskie, ne-komata). Rare names, place names and technical terms are the usual cases. Common function words ('to', 'also', 'not') get only weak to moderate activation.

Fires in JavaScript/TypeScript-style code on the token that opens a function or block body: '{⏎' after an arrow '=>' or after a function signature, the '=>' itself, and the indentation at the start of the first line inside a new block. Arrow-function bodies fire strongest. Other code punctuation (';⏎', '}⏎⏎', a quote-comma-newline) fires moderately to weakly, and prose does not fire.

Fires on a mid-word subword piece or a number/letter piece inside a proper name, place name or label, where the rest of the token is highly predictable: Vo[iv]odeship, T[ama]ulipas, [Hart]mut, LY[5]1, K-[2], 3[ m] springboard, Under 18's. Sports, biographical and geographic entity text is common. Ordinary words in running prose barely fire.

Fires on the first subword piece of a word, often a capitalized word in a heading or a legal/proper-name context ('Fi'anna Fáil, 'Conf'ederate/'Conf'essions, 'Acc'ompaniment, APP-ELLATE, CRIM-INAL in court captions), and on Czech/Polish diacritic pieces (ř, ą). It also fires on some verbs that follow a subject ('conducting', 'took', 'received'). The token being a word-start fragment of a longer word matters most.

Fires on the AM/PM marker right after a clock time (e.g. '6:40[[ AM]]', '10:26[[pm]]'), in any case and with or without a space, as in email headers and post timestamps. It fires weaker on other short capital-letter or 2-3 letter pieces after a name or abbreviation (MOTU, MSU, MTI, Makefile.am, '£25pm').

Fires on tokens in non-English text, strongest on short function words or word starts in Czech, German, Russian, Danish, Vietnamese and similar languages (' v', ' so', 'Как', ' Jeg', ' люб', ' không'). It is weaker on subword pieces of foreign names and words embedded in English. English prose fires little.

Fires on a token in the middle of a fixed multi-token term or identifier, where the token continues a known compound: 'Miss' New York, 'partial' pressure, 'ejection' fraction, 'angina p-ector-is', 'front'-runner, 'T3[N]0M0', 'tableOutput', 'VideoMode', 'docker run -it -p', 'Register with'. The term can be medical, code or a set phrase. Examples are very heterogeneous, so no single context reliably predicts it.

Fires on verbs of speaking or conversing in interview-style framing ('got to speak/talk with', 'I spoke to', 'speaking with', 'will speak at'). A related offshoot is survey/interview vocabulary ('question'-naires, 'Th-ematic analysis', 'answer'). Separately it fires on the first letter piece of an email handle or username ('j'entschura@, @'j'ulie_kelly, 't'shimura@), plus some Danish word pieces.

Fires in source code on the first statement keyword of a new line inside a block, above all 'if' (also 'while', 'else if', '.then'), right after the line's indentation. It fires moderately on other identifier pieces and tokens inside code (function names, numeric suffixes). Prose does not fire.

Fires strongest on the space token between an abbreviated month name and a day or year ('Jan[[ ]]01', 'Feb[[ ]]20', 'Aug[[ ]]2018', 'JUL[[ ]]18') and on 'Fig[[ ]]1'. It also fires on assorted mid-word pieces (blastosp-ores, Col-oured, St-over). Sentence-ending periods fire moderately.

Fires on the final token that completes a common fixed multi-word expression or compound: face-to-'face', one-on-'one', head-'on', 'Non-human', 'a great time', 'of all things', 'FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE', and 'to' in 'need to / space to / set out to / the words to'. The predictability of the token given the phrase so far matters most. Odd subword pieces of URLs and names also fire.

Fires on 'the' in license boilerplate 'See the License / See the LICENSE file', and on the last piece of a multi-token word or name (oil-seed, conserv-ing, Parapleg-ic, Epile-psy, N.J, programmed death). Many top examples are completions of predictable compounds. Other uses of 'the' fire weakly to moderately.

Fires on the first word of the body text right after a title or question heading, especially 'I have' after a 'Q:' title, 'Okay', 'Say', 'Theorem', 'A:'. It also fires on early tokens of a document's opening sentence ('It is a truism that'). Activation is moderate (about 45%) for most of these and peaks on a lone 'Okay' after an 'update' line. Tokens deep inside paragraphs barely fire.

Fires on a word-initial 'l'/'L' token or a piece beginning with l ('l'ato, 'L'GA, 'L'inq, 'l'izards, 'l'atte, 'lo'athe, 'low', 'Lo'ops), that is, when the word starts with a lone L-piece followed by the rest of the word. The token identity (starts with l) matters most.

Fires on the word right after a subject (often 'I', 'you', 'the user') that begins a modal or verb phrase: 'can', 'want', 'need', 'will', 'should', 'can only', 'To better'. It is a predicate-start position within a clause. It also fires on prepositions after a noun ('in', 'on', 'in terms'). Punctuation and nouns fire weakly.

Fires on punctuation and operator tokens in code, markup and structured data: commas inside SVG path data, '<' in comparisons and class inheritance, '[' in LaTeX theorem definitions, '/' in Enron email paths, ':' after a speaker name, '=' and 'import'. Moderate cases are other separators in tables, CSV or citations. Plain words fire weakly.

Fires on the token right after a number: units ('percent', 'mM', 'px', '%', 'ago'), or a single-digit reference numeral in patent text ('screw [2]24', 'envelope [3]'). It also fires on some suffix/abbreviation pieces (AHL, EUV, subcut-aneous, Battle-front). A wider scatter of weaker hits on prose tokens makes it partly a mixture.

Fires on predictable completions of boilerplate and fixed phrases, above all 'notice' in 'retain the above copyright notice', 'License' in 'Apache License', 'Inc', 'nonexclusive'. Other cases are 'nearest' in 'Round ... to the nearest', 'every' in 'one ... for every', 'DOCTYPE' after '<!', '.css'. Strength tracks how formulaic the preceding context makes the token.

Fires on the first subword piece of a word split into several tokens, especially pieces like 'unt' (untold, untimely, untie), 'Dup', 'dub', 'det', 'Den', 't' (in t.co links, tibial). The word is usually rarer or technical and broken into pieces at its start. Common whole words do not fire.

Fires on a grab-bag of tokens in code, legal and license boilerplate: package-name pieces (quark-us, kubef-ake), struct-field indentation, 'ORDER' in court captions, 'the'/'IMPLIED'/'ownership' in license headers, and also some ordinary prose ('wait for', 'Lanes is'). No single shared feature is evident.
